note — the bold part is what the card te: für always takes the accusative: der Vater → meinen Vater.

English: I'm buying a cake for **my brother**.
German: Ich kaufe einen Kuchen für **meinen Bruder**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: für + accusative: meinen Bruder.
die-words do not change: für meine Mutter.

English: I need the car for **one day**.
German: Ich brauche das Auto für **einen Tag**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: für with a length of time: für einen Tag.
ohne takes the accusative: seinen Mantel.
ohne + a noun with no article: ohne Zucker, ohne Milch.
ohne: without. Like English, no article here.
durch takes the accusative: der Park → den Park.
durch die Stadt: die stays die.
laufen changes au to äu: er läuft. durch den Wald: accusative.
der Wald → den Wald after durch.
durch: along and through, from one end to the other.
gegen: against, also hitting something. der Baum → einen Baum.

English: The children are playing against **the parents**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: gegen + accusative; the plural die stays die.

English: On Saturday we play against **your team**. (several friends)
German: Am Samstag spielen wir gegen **euer Team**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: gegen + accusative: das Team → euer Team, no ending.
gegen before a time means roughly: around eight. um acht would be exactly at eight.
um as a place means around: um die Ecke, with the accusative.

English: The children are running around **the table**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: um + accusative: der Tisch → den Tisch.
ich as the object becomes mich.
mich: me, the object.
du as the object becomes dich.
für takes the accusative, so für dich.
ohne + accusative: dich.
er as the object becomes ihn. nicht comes after the pronoun.
ihn: him.
ohne + accusative: ihn.
A der-word is ihn as an object, even a thing.

English: How do you like the film? (one friend) – I like **it**.
German: Wie findest du den Film? – Ich finde **ihn** gut.
note — the bold part is what the card te: der Film → ihn: the pronoun follows the noun's gender, not English it.
sie stays sie as the object.
A die-word is sie as an object too.
A das-word is es, as subject or object.

English: She loves him, and he loves **her**.
German: Sie liebt ihn, und er liebt **sie**.
note — the bold part is what the card te: sie does not change in the accusative; er does: ihn.

English: Are you visiting **us** on Sunday? (one friend)
note — the bold part is what the card te: wir as the object becomes uns.
gegen + accusative: uns.
ihr as the object becomes euch.
für + accusative: euch.
Formal Sie does not change in the accusative.
sie (they) as the object is still sie.
